before: Arts centre with galleries, theatres and a cafe bar at 10 Exchange Street West, in Belfast's Cathedral Quarter, opposite St Anne's Cathedral (MAC website; Wikipedia).

It is the successor to the Old Museum Arts Centre, which opened in 1989 and closed at the end of January 2010. The Metropolitan Arts Centre (the MAC) opened on 20 April 2012 (Wikipedia). It is a registered charity, NIC100808.

Building: designed by the Belfast firm Hackett Hall McKnight, completed in February 2012, with intersecting brick volumes and a basalt tower topped by glazing. It won a 2013 RIBA National Award and the 2014 Downes Medal (Wikipedia). The capital development cost £18m (Museums Association).
On site: art exhibitions, theatre, dance, comedy, a family programme, a cafe bar, creative learning and venue hire. Its one permanent artwork is "The Permanent Present" by Mark Garry (Wikipedia).

Visiting: open Tuesday to Sunday from 9am, galleries 11am to 5pm. The page lists no admission prices and links to a separate accessibility page. Wikipedia says the old centre's limited wheelchair access was a factor in the decision to build anew.

Visiting: open 11:00 to 18:00 on the day checked. Other days are not listed. Tickets €12, with reduced prices of €8, €5 and €0.

before: Non-collecting public art gallery in the former Centennial Planetarium, a Brutalist building with a geodesic dome roof completed in 1967 for the Canadian Centennial, at the edge of downtown Calgary (Wikipedia).

Formed in 2013 by the merger of three Calgary arts groups: the Institute of Modern and Contemporary Art, the Museum of Contemporary Art and the Art Gallery of Calgary. In June 2018 it agreed a 25-year lease of the building with the City of Calgary (Wikipedia).

The building housed a science centre (now TELUS Spark) from the 1980s until 2011. KPMB Architects' Bruce Kuwabara, with Gibbs Gage Architects, was chosen in January 2019 to lead the renovation (Wikipedia).

Opened two days a week in June 2019. Officially opened on 23 January 2020 with the group show "Planetary" and Luke Jerram's "Museum of the Moon". Closed in March 2020 and reopened in September 2020 (Wikipedia).
On site: the Observatory Gallery, the Dome Theatre and a smaller theatre, the Flanagan Family Gallery and the Ring Gallery around the Dome Theatre (Making & Meaning, 2024).

Visiting: open Wednesday to Saturday 12pm to 7pm and Sunday 12pm to 5pm, closed Monday and Tuesday. The gallery says it aims to be "free of physical, social, and financial barriers". No admission price or accessibility details are published on the pages read.

before: Contemporary art museum at 61 NE 41st Street in the Miami Design District, free every day.

before: Artist residency and contemporary art centre at 724 S. 12th Street in the Old Market Historic District of downtown Omaha, Nebraska.
Founded in 1981 by Jun Kaneko, Tony Hepburn, Lorne Falk and Ree Schonlau as "Alternative Worksite" (stated by the centre).

It was formerly housed in the Bemis Omaha Bag Company Building at 614 South 11th Street, severely damaged in a fire in 1999. In 1984 Schonlau set up a consortium of the City of Omaha, the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, private and corporate foundations and the Mercer family, who owned the vacant Bemis Bag Building (Wikipedia).

Its home since 1995 is a 100,000 sq. ft. former McCord-Brady wholesale grocery warehouse. A capital campaign launched in 2009 added five live/work studios and the 9,000 sq. ft. Okada Sculpture + Ceramics Facility, completed October 2011 (stated by the centre).

On site: exhibitions, private live/work residency studios, a Curator-in-Residence post (since 2017), a Sound Art + Experimental Music programme (since 2019) with the LOW END music venue, and public programmes.

Visiting: free admission to exhibitions and LOW END performances. Open Wednesday, Friday, Saturday and Sunday 11am to 5pm, Thursday 11am to 9pm, closed Monday and Tuesday. The centre states it is committed to accessible facilities. The Accessibility page was not read.

before: Museum of contemporary art in a former wool-spinning mill in Tilburg, North Brabant (Dutch Wikipedia; museum website).
Founded by the Stichting De Pont, a foundation set up in 1988 with part of the estate of Jan de Pont. The museum opened on 12 September 1992 (Dutch Wikipedia; museum website).
Named for the lawyer and businessman J.H. (Jan) de Pont, born in Tilburg on 22 February 1915, who died there on 18 September 1987 (museum website).

The mill belonged to Thomas de Beer, which De Pont helped restart in 1969. The foundation bought the closed property for a symbolic sum and Benthem Crouwel Architekten renovated it. Additions: a project space and auditorium in 2002 and a 1,100 square metre wing in 2016 (Dutch Wikipedia; museum website).
On site: galleries, with Anish Kapoor's "Sky Mirror" made for the 25th anniversary, and a collection that started with about ten works by three artists (Dutch Wikipedia; Omroep Brabant).
Hendrik Driessen directed it until 2019, Martijn van Nieuwenhuyzen followed, and Dutch Wikipedia states Maria Schnyder succeeded him in 2026.
Visiting: open Tuesday to Sunday 11am to 5pm, Thursday until 8pm, closed Monday. The homepage lists no ticket prices and links an accessibility statement that was not read.

before: Federal art museum at Albertinaplatz 1 in Vienna's Innere Stadt, with two further sites: Albertina Modern at Karlsplatz 5 and Albertina Klosterneuburg, which opened in April 2024.

The museum says the collection was founded in 1776 by Duke Albert of Saxony-Teschen and Archduchess Marie Christine. Building and collection passed into state ownership in April 1919 (German Wikipedia; English Wikipedia says early 1919) and the house was renamed the Albertina in 1921 (Wikipedia). Since 1 January 2000 it has been a scientific institution under public law and a federal museum (German Wikipedia).
Directors: Klaus Albrecht Schröder led it from 1999 to 2024. Ralph Gleis has been director general since 1 January 2025 (German Wikipedia).

Building: a former palace on a site that was part of Vienna's fortifications, extended by Louis Montoyer, heavily damaged by bombing in March 1945 and refurbished from 1998 to 2003. The "Soravia Wing" extension of 2003 drew mostly critical media reaction (Wikipedia, English and German). Albertina Modern occupies the former Künstlerhaus. The Hans Hollein roof over the entrance dates from 2008.

Collection: one of the world's largest print rooms, with about 65,000 drawings and roughly 1 million old master prints, plus photography and architectural drawings. The Batliner collection has been on long-term loan since 2007 and the Essl Collection of 1,323 works was acquired in 2018 (Wikipedia).

Nazi-era history: works stolen from Jewish collectors entered the collection after the 1938 Anschluss. After the war the museum contested restitution claims for works by Klimt and Schiele, and its director called for a moratorium on claims (English Wikipedia).

Visiting: the main site is open daily 10am to 6pm, until 9pm on Wednesday and Friday. Albertina Klosterneuburg is open Thursday to Sunday 10am to 5pm. The museum had 1,321,385 visits in 2024 (German Wikipedia). Admission prices were not on the pages read. The museum publishes an accessibility statement and an easy-read page.

before: Non-profit contemporary art foundation in a former tile factory in the Old City of Jerusalem, near the New Gate and the Collège des Frères school.

Founded in 1998 by Jack Persekian, an artist and curator, after his Anadiel Gallery (opened in the early 1990s on Salah al-Din Street, moved to the Old City in 1996) and its circle decided to open a contemporary art foundation (Jerusalem Story, 12 September 2024). Persekian is named as director in Gulf News (2018). The Jerusalem Story piece lists Shireen Mufdi as deputy director.
Named al-Ma'mal, Arabic for "factory," after the tile factory.

Building: a Palestinian hand-painted tile factory founded in 1900 by the Kassissieh family. It closed in the mid-1970s after the Jerusalem Municipality withdrew licences for Old City factories and stood abandoned until the mid-1990s (Jerusalem Story). Gulf News reports the family leased it to the group for 20 years, in exchange for paying the taxes owed and renovating it. Renovation began in 1998, and Israel's Antiquities Authority fined the group and took it to court for lacking a construction permit, which the article says Palestinians almost never obtain (Gulf News).

What is there: exhibition and multipurpose halls, a library, a rooftop garden with a stage, a basement with glass floors showing archaeological remains, and an artist residence. Programmes: residencies, exhibitions, film training, art classes in schools, concerts, and the Jerusalem Show, which has joined the Qalandiya International biennial.
Visiting: the site gives no opening hours or admission and states no accessibility details. The pages read cover venue hire only.

before: Public art museum at 1040 Moss Street, about 20 minutes from downtown Victoria (Tourism Victoria).
Founded in 1946 as the Little Centre by former members of the Federation of Canadian Artists' Vancouver Island branch. It ran from a former downtown car dealership until 1951 (Wikipedia).

In 1951 Sarah Spencer donated Spencer Mansion and the gallery took its present name. The house, built in 1889 to designs by William Ridgeway Wilson for the Green family, was called Gyppeswyk (Wikipedia).
Seven modernist galleries were added between 1955 and 1978. Renovations in 2001 to 2003 added climate control (Wikipedia).

A 2015 expansion design by LWPAC and Moore Architecture drew Mayor Lisa Helps' word "startling" (Attractions Management). Construction planned for late 2019 was postponed over rising costs (Wikipedia).
The collection holds about 20,000 works, the largest of any BC art museum, including about 8,000 Asian works. The garden holds the only Meiji-era Shinto shrine in North America (Wikipedia).
Its summer street festival, the Paint-In, draws 40,000 visitors annually (Tourism Victoria). No reporting found of current hours, admission or accessibility, as the gallery's site could not be read.

before: Sculpture museum at 1121 Ninohira, Hakone, Kanagawa Prefecture (museum website).

The Chokoku no Mori Art and Culture Foundation says it was launched on 6 September 1968 as the Chokoku no Mori Museum foundation, that the museum opened on 1 August 1969 as Japan's first open-air museum devoted to sculpture, and that it became a public interest foundation on 1 April 2012 (foundation website, translated from Japanese). Japanese Wikipedia gives the opening as 6 September 1969.

The foundation says it was established by the Fujisankei Group, centred on Fuji Television, Sankei Shimbun and Nippon Broadcasting System (foundation website). The museum website names Nobutaka Shikanai as its founder and first director, who aimed to "contribute to the development of sculpture" because no museum devoted to sculpture existed in Japan. Japanese Wikipedia calls him chairman of the Fujisankei Group.
The sculptor Takeshi Inoue was commissioned for the museum and grounds (museum website).

The museum holds a little over 2,000 works, and has held 21 international sculpture competitions to build the collection (museum website). English Wikipedia names Picasso, Henry Moore and Taro Okamoto among the artists and describes a Picasso Pavilion with about 300 works.
The foundation opened a sister museum, the Utsukushigahara Open-Air Museum in Ueda, Nagano, in 1981 (foundation website).

Visiting: open 9:00 to 17:00 every day of the year. General admission is 2,000 yen at the counter and 1,800 yen with a web ticket, university and high school students 1,600 yen, junior high and elementary students 800 yen, preschool children free. Visitors with a disability certificate pay 1,000 yen and their students and younger visitors pay nothing. Wheelchairs and strollers can be borrowed free at the information desks (museum website).

Private art museum in Kurashiki, Okayama prefecture. The museum's history page calls it Japan's first private museum centred on Western art (translated from the Japanese).

Founded in 1930 by Magosaburo Ohara in memory of the painter Kojima Torajiro, who had died the year before. The building was completed on 5 November 1930 and Takeuchi Kiyomi was its first director (museum history page).
Kojima travelled to Europe three times at Ohara's urging and chose many of the core works, including pieces by El Greco, Gauguin, Monet and Matisse (museum website).
On site: the main gallery, the Craft and Oriental Hall and the Kojima Torajiro Memorial Museum, on one ticket (museum visitor page).

Visiting: closed Mondays (open if Monday is a public holiday, no closures in August). March to November 9:00 to 17:00, December to February 9:00 to 15:00, last entry 30 minutes before closing. Adults 2,000 yen, under 18 500 yen, preschoolers free, Kurashiki residents and workers 1,900 yen. People holding disability certificates enter free, and one companion with some grades. Wheelchairs and strollers can be borrowed free inside. The site links a separate accessibility page that was not read.

before: Duke University's art museum, at 2001 Campus Drive on Duke's central campus in Durham, North Carolina.

Named for Raymond D. Nasher, a Duke alumnus, Texas real estate developer and sculpture collector, who gave $7.5 million in 1998 for a new museum and died on 16 March 2007 (museum website).

Building: designed by Rafael Viñoly. The Wikipedia article gives a cost of $24 million. It stands on the former 8.8-acre meadow at Duke University Road and Anderson Street that Duke botanists used for research plants (INDY Week).
Collection: more than 13,000 works, including pre-Columbian objects and contemporary art by artists such as Kara Walker, Kehinde Wiley and Ai Weiwei (Wikipedia).
Directors: Michael Mezzatesta 1987 to 2003, Kim Rorschach 2004 to 2012, Sarah Schroth 2013 to 2020, Trevor Schoonmaker since May 2020 (Wikipedia).
Visiting: admission is free for all. The museum page showed hours of 12:00 to 17:00 on the day checked. The full schedule was not on the page read.

Building: designed by Herzog & de Meuron, its first project in Korea. Eleven floors above ground and five below, 8,167 m2 gross, with 2,981 m2 of exhibition space. The concrete facade is textured with larch plywood boards (SongEun website; Metalocus, 17 October 2021).

before: Contemporary art museum in Dolapdere, Beyoğlu, a working-class Istanbul neighbourhood (Qantara), run as a non-profit by the Vehbi Koç Foundation (VKV).

The 18,000 square metre building is by Grimshaw with Istanbul's Turgut Alton Architects, won in a competition. It has 3,000 square metres of galleries, a sculpture terrace and a facade of convex and concave rhomboid panels (The Art Newspaper, Grimshaw).
Inside: the 168-seat Sevgi Gönül Auditorium, the Karbon theatre for up to 332, a library, learning spaces, a bookshop and Bistro by Divan (Grimshaw, Arter).

The collection, started in 2007, holds more than 1,300 works, about half by Turkish artists. Ömer Koç, a third-generation Koç and collector, chairs Arter, and Melih Fereli is director (The Art Newspaper).
Entry was free for residents of the area in 2019 (Qantara). No reporting found of current hours or prices, as the site's visit pages could not be read.

before: International television series festival in Lille, held each March. The 2026 edition ran from 20 to 27 March, with a professional Forum from 24 to 26 March (festival website).

In December 2015 the then Culture Minister Fleur Pellerin asked Herszberg to create a major international series festival. Lille was chosen over Cannes, Bordeaux, Nice and Paris after a CNC call for applications, and the festival has been in Lille since 2018 (Wikipedia).
Lille venues include the Tripostal, the Nouveau Siècle, UGC cinemas and the CCI. The professional forum is at Lille Grand Palais (Wikipedia).
Attendance was above 85,000 in 2023, with nearly 4,000 accredited professionals from 64 countries (Wikipedia).
It also runs the Séries Mania Institute, launched in Lille in August 2021 for training in the series trades (CB News).
Visiting: the Village Festival by Crédit Mutuel at the Tripostal is free (Crédit Mutuel Nord Europe). No ticket prices were found on the pages opened.

before: State art museum at 6 Hrushevskoho Street, Kyiv, with a collection of more than 40,000 exhibits from the 12th century to the present (museum site).

First exhibition held in August 1899. Officially opened in December 1904 as the Kyiv Art-Industrial and Scientific Museum of Emperor Nikolai Alexandrovich. Renamed many times (the museum says 12 times). The current name dates from 1994 (Wikipedia; museum site).

Building completed in 1898, designed by Moscow architect Petro Boitsov and reworked by the Polish architect Wladyslaw Horodecki, with sculptural decoration attributed to Emilio Sala. Construction cost 249,000 rubles, of which 100,000 came from the imperial government and 108,000 from the Tereshchenko family (Wikipedia).
First director: Mykola Biliashivsky. The current director listed is Yulia Lytvynets (Wikipedia).

The permanent exhibition was removed on 24 February 2022 for security reasons. The museum runs temporary exhibition projects, and events pause during air raid alerts (museum site). Wikipedia states a Russian air attack on 24 May 2026 destroyed its windows and damaged its skylights and plaster walls.

Visiting: Thursday to Sunday 12:00 to 18:00. Full ticket UAH 150. Schoolchildren, students and pensioners UAH 100. Military personnel free. The site has a text-size and contrast menu. No step-free access details were found.

before: India's national academy of fine arts, headquartered at Rabindra Bhavan, Ferozshah Road, New Delhi, in a building shared with the Sangeet Natak Akademi and the Sahitya Akademi (Wikipedia).

Set up by the Government of India and inaugurated on 5 August 1954. Registered under the Societies Registration Act 1860 on 11 March 1957 (Akademi website). Maulana Azad, then Minister of Education, set it up (Wikipedia).
The name is Hindi for "fine arts academy". It is not named for a person.

Rabindra Bhavan holds its art galleries, which the Akademi lets artists book for exhibitions. The Akademi runs regional centres in Chennai, Lucknow, Kolkata, Bhubaneswar and Garhi (Delhi), with sub-centres at Shimla, Ahmedabad, Agartala and Patna. A new Kolkata centre building was inaugurated on 15 January 2026 (Akademi website).

Programmes: the annual National Exhibition of Art, the Triennale-India (run since 1968), scholarships and fellowships, a bilingual journal and the Garhi studios (Wikipedia). Its permanent collection holds over seven thousand artworks, including works by M.F. Husain, S.H. Raza and Somnath Hore (Akademi website).
Visiting: the reference library is open Monday to Friday, 9.30 a.m. to 6.00 p.m. The Akademi site does not state gallery hours, admission or accessibility on the pages read.

before: Municipal gallery of Bulgarian art at 1 General Gurko Street, Sofia, with its entrance from Knyaz Al. Batenberg Street (sghg.bg).

Began in 1928, when Mayor Vladimir Vazov decreed a commission to set up a municipal museum of Sofia with a museum, a library and an archive. A picture gallery was part of its work from the start (sghg.bg history).

Housing: various buildings from 1929. A purpose-built building opened in 1941 at 3 Banski Square and was destroyed in bombing. The gallery received its own space at 1 General Gurko Street in 1973, which opened in 1977. The library and archive separated in 1952 and the museum and the gallery became separate institutions (sghg.bg history).
Not named for a person.

What is there: four departments (painting, sculpture, graphics, contemporary art and photography) and a collection of more than 23,000 works by Bulgarian artists from the late 19th century to the present. Branches include the Vaska Emanouilova Gallery (opened 2006) and the Dechko Uzunov Gallery-Museum (2016). Some sculptures stand in the City Garden (sghg.bg history).

Programme example: the "Other Eye" project, launched in 2010, in which people who are not art historians curate shows from the permanent collection. "Portrait of a Friend" (2019) was its fifth, curated by the filmmaker Iglika Trifonova (Sofia Globe).

Visiting: Tuesday to Saturday 10:00 to 19:00, Sunday 11:00 to 18:00, closed Monday and on Christmas, New Year and Easter. Free on the second and fourth Thursday of each month. The gallery says the address is accessible to people with impaired motor functions. The ticket price is on a pricing page that was not read (sghg.bg).

before: 16 January 2024: the ministry revoked funding for the 2024 programme prepared by internal and external curators (the Kunsthalle's statement).

15 January 2024: director Jen Kratochvíl left his post. The ministry's spokesman Pavol Čorba said he asked Culture Minister Martina Šimkovičová to release him because he wanted to focus on curating and teaching (STVR, 17 January 2024).
Ministry reasoning: the Kunsthalle "did not use its historic opportunity" in programme content, public expectations and economic efficiency (Čorba, as reported by SITA, 17 January 2024).

The Kunsthalle's statement said cultural professionals were being accused of promoting values that endanger "the future of children in Slovakia", and voiced concern for the institution's independence and freedom.

Finestre sull'Arte (18 January 2024) describes the Kunsthalle's programming on feminism, queer culture, migration and support for the LGBT community, and reports that Šimkovičová said LGBTI+ groups "will no longer exploit the funds of the culture department as parasites." It names no exhibition as the cause of the funding cut.

Unverified: that the ministry forced Kratochvíl to resign and that the move under the SNG, with funding revoked, effectively shut the Kunsthalle down, from Eurozine (Tomáš Hučko, 2 December 2024). Erste Foundation CEO Boris Marte wrote on 9 September 2024 that Kratochvíl resigned due to the revocation of funding (the foundation's own site, an advocacy source).

before: Two exhibition venues for François Pinault's collection in Venice: Palazzo Grassi, and Punta della Dogana, a former customs house (Wikipedia; museum website).

Palazzo Grassi was rebuilt between 1748 and 1772 to a design by Giorgio Massari. The Fiat Group bought it in 1983 under Gianni Agnelli, and Gae Aulenti oversaw a restoration. Pinault bought it in May 2005 for 29 million euros (Wikipedia).

Tadao Ando remodelled Palazzo Grassi, which reopened in April 2006, and restored Punta della Dogana from January 2008 to March 2009. It opened in June 2009. Ando redesigned the Teatrino as a 225-seat auditorium in 2013 (Wikipedia).
The City of Venice owns the Punta della Dogana building (Wikipedia).

Current shows include "Lorna Simpson. Third Person" at Punta della Dogana (29 March to 22 November 2026) and "Michael Armitage. The Promise of Change" at Palazzo Grassi (29 March 2026 to 10 January 2027) (museum website).

Visiting: during exhibition periods open daily except Tuesdays, 10:00 to 18:00, last entry 17:00, closed 25 December. An accessible guide and an Italian Sign Language presentation are offered. The page lists no prices.

before: Design, architecture and art institution in the Palazzo dell'Arte in Parco Sempione, Milan, hosting the Milan Triennale international exhibition, the Museo del Design Italiano, a theatre and exhibitions (Wikipedia, Italian Wikipedia).

The first exhibition was held in 1923 at the Villa Reale in Monza. The Triennale moved to Milan in 1933, became an autonomous legal body in 1931, and resumed the International Exhibition in 2016 after a pause of about twenty years (Italian Wikipedia).

Palazzo dell'Arte was designed by Giovanni Muzio and built 1931 to 1933, financed by Antonio Bernocchi and his brothers Andrea and Michele (Wikipedia). A plaque records the Bernocchi family's donation of the palace to the city (Italian Wikipedia caption).
Exhibitions, a design museum, the Teatro dell'Arte and a project library (Italian Wikipedia).

Visiting: a search listing of the official site gives Tuesday to Sunday, exhibitions 10:30 to 20:00, last entry 19:00. Travel guides give museum admission of about EUR 15, which could not be checked on the official site.

before: Public museum of modern art at Guillem de Castro 118 in Valencia. The main building, the Centre Julio González, sits on remains of the city's medieval walls (Wikipedia, IVAM).

The Valencian government created the institute in 1986 and it opened in February 1989, the first modern art centre in Spain. Tomàs Llorens was its first director. A second site in the Centre del Carme ran until 2002 (Wikipedia).
The collection began with the Julio González holdings bought before opening and now has about 10,000 works, mainly 20th-century art and photography (Wikipedia).
Blanca de la Torre has directed it since 1 April 2025, after an international public competition (Valencia News).
In 2025 it had 202,258 visitors, 48 percent from abroad, and bought 16 works by 14 women artists for about €1 million (Valencia News).
Visiting: Tuesday to Sunday 10:00 to 19:00, closed Mondays. The home page gives no prices.

before: Private foundation and art centre in New Chamba Valley, Lusaka, with a gallery, a research library, an artist residency, a social room for talks and recordings, and two private spaces for visiting artists (Art Africa, January 2023; Artdependence, January 2023).

Founded by Victor Mutelekesha, a Zambian artist based in Oslo. He conceived the idea in December 2002 during a visit in Amsterdam, and the centre opened on 6 January 2023 (Nkwazi Magazine). It describes itself as Zambia's first contemporary art centre of its kind (Kunstkritikk, 2020).
Named for the city of Lusaka. LuCAC is its abbreviation.

Building: Mutelekesha bought the Lusaka plot with his own funds in the early 2000s. Main building construction began in March 2020 (Kunstkritikk, 2020) and took three years, delayed by COVID-19 (Nkwazi Magazine). Architect not named in the sources read.

What is there: the gallery, library, residency, a plan for workshops and seminars and an archive of its own activities. The inaugural exhibition "Prospice, Kwacha!", curated by Karen Reini, ran from 6 January to 17 December 2023 with Banji Chona, Sana Ginwalla, Daut Makala and Germain Ngoma (Art Africa, Nkwazi Magazine).
Visiting: Nkwazi Magazine (2023) gives hours of Tuesday to Saturday 10:00 to 17:00 and Sunday 12:00 to 16:00. No admission or accessibility information found.

before: Municipal house museum at Quintana 3900 in Mar del Plata, on grounds of natural area crossed by the Las Chacras stream (La Nación, El Economista).

Designed by Amancio Williams and Delfina Gálvez Bunge for his father, the musician and composer Alberto Williams. El Economista dates the commission to 1943, and the "Iconic Houses" network (iconichouses.org) dates the design to 1942 and completion to 1945.
Also called Casa del Puente, after the large curved arch known as "El Puente" that carries the house over the stream (El Economista).

Concrete structure, on a site of two blocks of natural area that the stream crosses. The radio station LU9 used the house from 1970 to 1977, and it then stood empty until 2004 (El Economista, La Nación).

A fire in 2004 destroyed the interior. The restoration covered about 450 square metres, the main house and the caretaker's house, and the house reopened on 20 April 2023 (iconichouses.org, El Economista).
Visiting: before the 2023 reopening La Capital described visits as groups with a prior booking, guided, limited to 10 to 15 people. No current opening days, admission or accessibility found.

before: Villa at Kundmanngasse 19 (the institute's address is Parkgasse 18) in Vienna's 3rd district, Landstraße, near the U3 station Rochusgasse (Wien Geschichte Wiki, haus-wittgenstein.at).

Built for Margaret Stonborough-Wittgenstein, who gave Paul Engelmann the commission in 1926 according to the institute and in autumn 1925 according to the Wien Geschichte Wiki and English Wikipedia. Her brother Ludwig Wittgenstein joined the planning and, the institute says, became the sole architect. The house was finished in 1928.
Named for Ludwig Wittgenstein. English Wikipedia also calls it Stonborough House.

Three storeys with the main floor 1.5 metres above the ground, bare grey-white surfaces and a horizontal emphasis, on a plot with old chestnut trees that Stonborough chose over a family plot on Renngasse. Inside, the floors are terrazzo and the walls stuccolustro, and no reporting found of the structural materials (institute).

Bulgaria bought the house in 1975 with half the garden. The other half was built over with a 14-storey Hauptverband der Sozialversicherungsträger office block after protests by architects stopped the hotel high-rise planned by the building contractor Franz Katlein (Wien Geschichte Wiki, German Wikipedia).

Today it holds the Bulgarian Cultural Institute, the cultural department of the Bulgarian Embassy, with a parterre gallery and monthly exhibitions, concerts, readings and lectures (haus-wittgenstein.at).

On site: the house, the park and the pool, with hire for shoots and events. Classified as a historic monument since 5 July 1996 and open to the public since 2007 (Wikipedia).

The page gives no accessibility details beyond reduced rates for disabled visitors.

Van Doesburg designed it with the building student Abraham Elzas, after the plan for a double house with Hans and Sophie Taeuber-Arp was dropped in 1927. It has a reinforced concrete frame and walls of compressed straw boards, plastered inside and coated with cement outside (Dutch Wikipedia).

Nelly lived there until 1975. Her niece Wies van Moorsel inherited it and gave it to the Dutch State in 1981 (Dutch Wikipedia).

before: Model house at Am Horn 61, Weimar, on a street of Gründerzeit villas. The plot had been a vegetable garden for the Bauhaus canteen (English Wikipedia).

Georg Muche designed it for the 1923 Bauhaus exhibition, and Walter Gropius's architecture office oversaw construction (Klassik Stiftung Weimar). The Berlin builder Adolf Sommerfeld financed it, by an interest-free loan according to English Wikipedia.
The name matches its address, Am Horn 61. No source found states how it was named.
One-storey house of steel and concrete with a flat roof. The walls have an outer concrete layer, a peat insulation layer and an inner lining (English Wikipedia).

After 1923 it changed hands. By 1951 the city of Weimar owned it, and it rented the house out until 1998. The Friends of the Bauhaus-Universität Weimar leased it from 1998 to 2017 and renovated it in 1998 and 1999. The Klassik Stiftung reopened it on 18 May 2019 after renovating since 2015 (Klassik Stiftung Weimar).
On site: rooms furnished as in 1923 with reconstructed furniture, and a media guide (Klassik Stiftung Weimar).

before: House museum and exhibition venue at Ebertstraße 26 in Zwenkau, in the Landkreis Leipzig (house's site).

The Zwenkau doctors Erna and Erich Rabe commissioned it from the architect Adolf Rading, who designed it in 1929 and 1930 (L-IZ, Vielfalt der Moderne). German Wikipedia gives 1929 to 1931. Authorities first rejected the design as "undeutsch" (German Wikipedia).
Named for the Rabe family. No earlier name found.

A three-storey cube with a two-storey living hall, etched street-side glass and coloured linoleum floors. Rading originally planned tubular steel furniture. Oskar Schlemmer designed the interior art, including a four-part metal composition and a five-metre profile head of sheet copper (Vielfalt der Moderne).

The Rabe family practised in the house until 1965 and their daughter ran the practice until 1991. Erna Rabe, who was Jewish, was deported to Theresienstadt on 13 February 1945 and survived. The art patron Horst Schmitter bought the house in 1994, and it was renovated in 1995 and 1996 and again in 2017 and 2018 (German Wikipedia).
On site: guided tours of the house, events for up to 15 people, a shop, and a Haus Rabe Circle of friends (house's site).

before: Villa at Parkstraße 58 in Chemnitz, in the Helbersdorf locality (English Wikipedia, C3 site).
The textile manufacturer Herbert Esche (1874 to 1962) commissioned it from Henry van de Velde. It was built in 1902 and 1903 and extended in 1911 (English Wikipedia).

before: Museum in the former studio, home and planned museum of the sculptor Gustav Vigeland at Nobels gate 32 in Frogner, south of Vigeland Park (museum site).

In 1919 Oslo City Council decided to build him a studio. In a contract of February 1921 he left all his works to the city and kept the right to use the studio until his death. He moved in in 1924, died there in 1943, and the museum opened in 1947 (museum site).
Named for Vigeland. No earlier name found.

Lorentz Harboe Ree, with his partner Carl Buch, designed the neoclassical red-brick building, with a courtyard fountain, colonnades and 13 exhibition halls. The sources give different construction years (lokalhistoriewiki: 1920 to 1928, whole complex 1932; English Wikipedia: begun 1921, south wing 1930). Riksantikvaren protected it on 8 April 2015 (lokalhistoriewiki).
On site: about 1,600 sculptures, 420 woodcuts, 12,000 drawings, letters, a library and photographs, plus the artist's apartment and a permanent exhibition running to 31 December 2026 (museum site).

Some art critics have read Vigeland's sculptures as fascist in style, and the Quisling regime published his 1944 reply on opening his studio to German visitors. The museum's senior curator Tone Wikborg is quoted as saying this does not make him a sympathiser of any political system (English Wikipedia, citing Slagstad 2008, Gauguin 1945 and Wikborg 2019; the originals were not read).

before: House museum at 4 Westmoreland Place in Pasadena, on a knoll above the Arroyo Seco (gamblehouse.org, English Wikipedia).

The house, dated 1908, was built by architects Charles and Henry Greene for David and Mary Gamble of the Procter and Gamble Company. The site calls it the most complete and original example of the Greenes' work (gamblehouse.org). Named for the Gambles. No earlier name found.

The Gamble family gave the house to the City of Pasadena in 1966 under a family gift agreement, and it has been open to the public since then. It is owned by the City and operated by The Gamble House Conservancy, a non-profit formed in 2019 (gamblehouse.org, Form 990). USC's School of Architecture ran it before that (English Wikipedia).
Interior wood is teak, maple, oak, Port Orford cedar and mahogany. The exterior is brick, stucco and granite river stones. National Historic Landmark since 22 December 1977 (English Wikipedia).
On site: the house, gardens and a bookstore (gamblehouse.org).

Visiting: open Tuesdays and Thursdays to Sundays, closed Mondays and Wednesdays. The bookstore is open 10:00 to 16:00 on touring days. Tours are guided, including a one-hour docent tour, and walk-up tickets are sold in the bookstore. Discounts: 50 percent off for members of listed museum associations, 10 percent off for AAA cards and veterans, free for active military, and free for up to four people with a SNAP card. Visitors should wear broad-heeled shoes or flats, and guests without them are given booties. Accessibility: limited first-floor access for manual wheelchairs by a staff-operated stair lift, no access for electric wheelchairs, stairs at the front entrance, 18 stairs to the second floor and 17 to the attic (gamblehouse.org).

It is owned by the City and operated by The Gamble House Conservancy, a non-profit formed in 2019 (gamblehouse.org, Form 990). USC's School of Architecture ran it before that (English Wikipedia).
Interior wood is teak, maple, oak, Port Orford cedar and mahogany. The exterior is brick, stucco and granite river stones. National Historic Landmark since 22 December 1977 (English Wikipedia).
On site: the house, gardens and a bookstore (gamblehouse.org).

Visiting: open Tuesdays and Thursdays to Sundays, closed Mondays and Wednesdays. The bookstore is open 10:00 to 16:00 on touring days. Tours are guided, including a one-hour docent tour, and walk-up tickets are sold in the bookstore. Discounts: 50 percent off for members of listed museum associations, 10 percent off for AAA cards and veterans, free for active military, and free for up to four people with a SNAP card. Visitors should wear broad-heeled shoes or flats, and guests without them are given booties. Accessibility: limited first-floor access for manual wheelchairs by a staff-operated stair lift, no access for electric wheelchairs, stairs at the front entrance, 18 stairs to the second floor and 17 to the attic (gamblehouse.org).

before: Garden and three houses (Turn End, Middle Turn and The Turn) at Townside in the centre of Haddenham, Buckinghamshire, 3 miles north-east of Thame and 5 miles south-west of Aylesbury (the Trust's site).

The architect Peter Aldington designed the houses and built them with his wife Margaret between 1964 and 1968, including their own home Turn End. The Aldington family and founder trustees formed the Turn End Trust in 1998, and it became a charitable incorporated organisation in 2015 (the Trust's site, Find that Charity).
Named for its main house, Turn End. No reporting found of where the name comes from.

Wood, concrete block and glass houses in a traditional village setting, with a garden of under an acre. The houses won a RIBA Award in 1970 and were listed Grade II* in 2006, and the garden was listed Grade II in 2017 (the Trust's site).
Margaret Aldington lives at Turn End, Middle Turn is privately owned and occupied, and The Turn is let. Peter Aldington died on 15 April 2026 aged 93 (the Trust's site, Building Design).

Visiting: no regular opening hours. The Trust runs public open days and events (the 24 May 2026 open day was cancelled), and groups of 10 or more can visit the garden, not the house, at £14.50 a person. There is no visitor parking, the house has one step at the entrance and three to an upper level, and the garden has gravel paths and several steps (the Trust's site).

before: Micro-museum at the Isokon Flats, Lawn Road, London NW3 2XD, in the building's former garage (the gallery's site).

The gallery opened in 2014 and is run by The Isokon Gallery Trust, which Find that Charity records as registered as a charitable incorporated organisation on 26 March 2015. It is staffed by volunteers.
The gallery tells the story of the Isokon Flats, and Jack Pritchard created the Isokon furniture company in the early 1930s (the gallery's site). No reporting found of how the name Isokon arose.

The flats, also called the Lawn Road Flats, were created by Jack and Molly Pritchard and the architect Wells Coates and opened in 1934. Avanti Architects refurbished them in 2003 for Notting Hill Housing Association, which bought them from Camden Council (the gallery's site, English Wikipedia).
On site: a permanent exhibition with a recreated dressing room and kitchen, a seasonal display each year, a shop and events (the gallery's site).

Visiting: free entry, 11 am to 4 pm Saturday and Sunday from March to the end of November and on the last Friday of each month. A flat is shown on some Sundays for a £10 donation, and the pages read give no accessibility information (the gallery's site).

before: Artist-run platform for contemporary art, culture and critical thought, started by Anton Vidokle in 1998 as an e-mail announcement list, a month after the exhibition 'The Best Surprise is No Surprise' at the Holiday Inn in Chinatown (Wikipedia). E-flux's own site dates the start to 1999. Julieta Aranda joined in 2003 and Brian Kuan Wood in 2008 as journal editor.

Vidokle was born in Moscow in 1965 and grew up near VDNKh. His family emigrated to New York in the early 1980s, when he was 15 (The Blueprint, Nika Komarova, 15 February 2022; Art Focus Now, 2 February 2022).

Addresses: a one-room apartment at 344A Greenwich Street (1998 to 2003), a storefront at 41 Essex Street (2008), 311 East Broadway with exhibition, office and event space (2011), and since December 2021 a building at 172 Classon Avenue, Brooklyn, which houses the 100-seat e-flux Screening Room (Wikipedia; e-flux website).

Programmes: announcement services (Announcements, Agenda, Architecture, Education, Film), the free monthly e-flux journal since 2008 (141 issues by December 2023), Notes, Criticism, Architecture, a podcast since 2018, books with Sternberg Press and University of Minnesota Press, the quarterly print e-flux Index (2024), an archive of over 60,000 announcements and texts, and screenings, talks, exhibitions and performances including projects at documenta and the Venice Biennale (e-flux website).

Earlier projects: e-flux video rental (2004, over 950 videos, donated in 2010 to Moderna galerija, Ljubljana), the Martha Rosler Library (2007), unitednationsplaza in Berlin, Pawnshop (2008), Time/Bank (2010) and SUPERCOMMUNITY for the 56th Venice Biennale (Wikipedia).

Bar Laika by e-flux opened on 18 October 2018 at 224 Greene Avenue, Clinton Hill, designed by Nikolaus Hirsch and Michel Müller, with drinks, screenings, talks and music (e-flux announcement, 12 October 2018).
Vidokle was named an Art Basel Awards medalist in the awards' second year (Art Basel, 7 October 2026).

e-flux Index launched on 10 May 2024 at KW Institute for Contemporary Art, Berlin, meta-edited by George MacBeth, designed by Remco van Bladel, issue 1 of 420 pages (later issues about 560), sold at e-flux.com and Walter König stores. Institutional subscriptions carry four print issues a year and digital downloads (e-flux announcements, 2024).

Companies on the New York register: E-FLUX, INC. (business corporation, filed 6 January 1999, Vidokle chairman), E-FLUX PROJECTS (not-for-profit, 2006), E-FLUX REALTY, LLC (2015) and ART DOMAIN, LLC, which runs Bar Laika (2015) (NY Department of State).
172 Classon Avenue, a 27,653 sq ft light-manufacturing building of 1931, belongs to 172 Classon Corp., not to e-flux. The city deed register names no e-flux company on it (ACRIS; PropertyShark).
